options: A sequence of tokens, each with a kind and a position
A tree, with the operators at the branches
A symbol table
Machine code for the target
drills.why: The lexer turns characters into words. Structure appears in the next step, when the parser turns that flat sequence into a tree.

drills.q: How does a lexer decide where one token ends and the next begins?
options: It takes the longest sequence of characters that forms a valid token
It takes the shortest token that lets the whole line parse
It asks the parser which token would fit
It splits on whitespace
drills.why: Maximal munch, applied at each position with no reference to meaning. It is the whole of the lexer's decision procedure.

drills.q: How does a C lexer split a+++b?
options: a, ++, +, b
a, +, ++, b
a, +, +, +, b
It is a syntax error before any splitting happens
drills.why: Longest match at each position. The first two plus characters make ++, which leaves a single + before b, so it compiles as (a++) + b.

drills.q: Why does every C compiler reject a+++++b?
options: Maximal munch gives (a++)++, and a++ is not an lvalue
The expression is ambiguous, so the compiler refuses to choose
Five operators in a row exceed the grammar's nesting limit
Increment cannot be applied to a variable twice in one statement
drills.why: The lexer produces ++, ++, + and never reconsiders. A human can see that a++ + ++b would work, and the compiler does not look for it, which is why the error is about the increment rather than about the tokenization.

drills.q: Before C++11, why did a vector of vectors need a space between the closing brackets?
options: >> is a longer valid token than >, so maximal munch produced the shift operator
The parser could not nest template arguments
Two closing brackets were reserved for the preprocessor
The standard library header did not support it
drills.why: The same rule as a+++b, in a place people met daily. C++11 fixed it in the parser rather than the lexer: the token is still >>, and the parser is required to treat it as two brackets inside a template argument list.

drills.q: What is 2 - 3 - 4 in C, and why?
options: -5, because subtraction groups to the left
3, because subtraction groups to the right
-5, because the compiler evaluates arguments left to right
Unspecified, because the order of evaluation is not defined
drills.why: Associativity decides the grouping, and grouping decides the answer. Order of evaluation is a different question and does not change this one.

drills.q: After the parser has built the tree, where does precedence live?
options: In the shape of the tree
In a table the later passes consult
In the order of the tokens, which the tree preserves
In parentheses, which the tree keeps for that purpose
drills.why: a + b * c becomes an addition whose right child is a multiplication. No later pass has to know the rule, because the grouping is now structure.

drills.q: In a precedence climbing parser, what is the difference between a left-associative and a right-associative operator?
options: The binding power used for the recursive call, by one
A separate function per associativity
The direction the token stream is read in
Nothing; associativity is fixed up after the tree is built
drills.why: Recurse with the same binding power and the operator leans right; recurse with one higher and it leans left. That is the whole difference.

drills.q: In C, what is A * B; at statement level?
options: A declaration if A is a typedef name, and a multiplication otherwise
Always a multiplication, because a declaration needs a storage class
Always a declaration, because a bare multiplication has no effect
Ambiguous, and the compiler picks either one
drills.why: The same four tokens are two different programs, and which one they are depends on a declaration that appeared earlier, possibly in a header. This is what makes the language context sensitive.

options: Feeding the symbol table back into the front end so a typedef name lexes as its own token kind
A workaround for compilers that cannot handle deeply nested parentheses
Preprocessing the file twice to resolve macros before parsing
Guessing the parse and backtracking when type checking fails
drills.why: The name is unfair, because there is no way to avoid it. The language is context sensitive, so the parser has to be too.

drills.q: What does Widget w(); declare inside a function?
options: A function named w taking nothing and returning a Widget
A default-constructed Widget named w
Nothing; it is a statement with no effect
A Widget initialised with the result of calling w
drills.why: Anything that could be a declaration is a declaration. It is the case that looks least like one, and it is the one people write by accident.

drills.q: Why was Widget w{}; added in C++11?
options: Braces cannot be read as a parameter list, so the construction is unambiguous
Braces initialise members in declaration order and parentheses do not
Parentheses were deprecated for construction
It compiles faster, because the parser has less to consider
drills.why: Giving people an escape from the most vexing parse is a large part of why the syntax exists.

drills.q: Inside a template, how does T::x * y; parse without typename?
options: As a multiplication, because a dependent name is assumed not to be a type
As a declaration, because that reading is preferred everywhere in C++
It depends on what T turns out to be at instantiation
It is rejected until the template is instantiated
drills.why: The parse is fixed when the template is parsed, long before any T exists, so the standard picks a default and gives you a keyword to override it.

drills.q: Why do C++ compilers have a template instantiation depth limit?
options: Instantiation is Turing complete, so deciding validity can require a computation that never finishes
The parser's stack is a fixed size
Deeper instantiation produces code too large to link
The standard specifies an exact maximum depth
drills.why: It is the halting problem arriving from a new direction. The limit is a compiler choosing to stop rather than run forever on a question with no general answer.

drills.q: What does an abstract syntax tree drop that a parse tree keeps?
options: Productions that existed only for the parser, such as parentheses and most punctuation
The operators, which move into a separate table
Source positions, which are no longer needed after parsing
Identifiers, which are replaced by symbol table indices
drills.why: It keeps what carries meaning. Clang deliberately keeps more than that, including parentheses and every source location, which is what makes clang-format and clang-tidy possible.
